Declare a co-stressor for a failure-rate hazard model

Source: R/discrete-time-hazard-brms.R
costressor.Rd

Describes one non-temperature environmental variable (Z) the individual is exposed to and that co-determines the failure rate: dissolved oxygen, salinity, pH, a toxicant concentration, or, for a terrestrial ectotherm, humidity. The failure rate then becomes a surface M(T, Z). The co-stressor enters log M(T) as its own term and, when asked for with interaction = TRUE, an interaction with temperature, so a crossed temperature-by-stressor design (a ramp run at two or more stressor levels) can estimate how the stressor changes the thermal response. Build one for each co-stressor and pass them together, as a list, to build_hazard_data, build_hazard_spec, build_hazard_prior and fit_hazard, so all four read the same declaration.

Usage

costressor(
  name,
  column,
  ref,
  scale,
  direction,
  interaction = FALSE,
  trajectory = NULL,
  transform = NULL
)

Arguments

name

A character string, a short name for the co-stressor, used to name its column (z_<name>) and its parameters (c<name>, dT<name>). Letters and digits only, starting with a letter, because brms allows no dot or underscore in a parameter name. For example "DO" gives the column z_DO and the parameters cDO and dTDO.

column

A character string naming the column that holds the raw measurement X: a column of ind (one value per individual) for a stressor held fixed within a trial, or a column of trajectory for one that changes over the trial.

ref

The benign, no-additional-stress reference level of the raw measurement (air-saturation for dissolved oxygen, zero for a toxicant, the control level for salinity or pH). The failure rate reduces to the pure M(T) here.

scale

A single positive number, the unit a coefficient is expressed per (per mg/L or per kPa for oxygen, per unit concentration for a toxicant).

direction

Either 1 or -1, set so that a positive z always means more stress: -1 for dissolved oxygen (less oxygen is more stress), 1 for a toxicant (more is more stress).

interaction

A single logical value. When FALSE (the default) the co-stressor enters through its main effect alone, changing the failure rate by the same proportion at every temperature. When TRUE it also enters through a temperature interaction dT<name>, so it can change the temperature slope of log M. For a multiplicative alternative that rescales thermal sensitivity instead, see ‘Two kinds of temperature interaction’ below, and for what an interaction implies outside the temperatures of the data, see ‘An interaction outside the temperatures of the data’.

trajectory

An optional data frame giving the co-stressor over time, with columns path_id, time and the column named above, in the shape of the path argument of build_hazard_data. Supply it for a stressor that changes during a trial; it is interpolated to the same interval midpoints as temperature. Leave NULL for a stressor held fixed within a trial, which is then read from ind.

transform

An optional function of the standardised deviation (X - ref) / scale that returns the column z. Use it for a stressor whose harm is not signed-linear, for example a squared deviation for a U-shaped response to salinity or pH, where a departure either way is harmful. When NULL (the default) the signed-linear deficit direction * (X - ref) / scale is used.

Value

A costressor object: a named list holding the declaration, for the costressors argument of build_hazard_data, build_hazard_spec, build_hazard_prior and fit_hazard.

Details

The raw measurement X becomes a standardised column z = direction * (X - ref) / scale, which is zero at the benign reference. There the failure rate reduces to the pure thermal M(T): the amplitude loga and critical temperature Tc keep their unstressed meaning, and a model with the co-stressor held at its reference is the same as one without it. This follows from centring the column at a chosen reference rather than at the sample mean.

The three pieces the standardisation needs (a reference, a scale, and a direction) are all required, as none has a safe default. A domain-chosen scale (per mg/L of oxygen, per unit concentration) is preferred to a data standard deviation, which is unstable with only two or three treatment levels. As an example, for dissolved oxygen with a reference at air-saturation (ref = 8.5 mg/L), a scale of 1 mg/L (scale = 1), and less oxygen meaning more stress (direction = -1), z = -1 * (X - 8.5) / 1 = 8.5 - X, the oxygen deficit is: z = 0 at saturation and z = 2.5 at 6 mg/L (below saturation). The direction re-orients every stressor onto a common axis on which a larger z always means more stress, so the main effect c<name> has the same sign meaning for every stressor: a positive value is a hazard that rises under stress.

This signed-linear column assumes the stressor harm runs one way. For a stressor that is harmful in either direction (salinity or pH, where a departure above or below the optimum both add stress), supply a transform function so z measures distance from the reference rather than a signed deficit: a squared standardised deviation, transform = function(u) u^2, makes z = ((X - ref) / scale)^2, zero at the optimum and rising on both sides. The direction then no longer applies, since z is symmetric.

The co-stressor contributes one or two parameters, named from name. The main effect c<name> is the change in the log failure rate per scale of stressor beyond the reference, and the interaction dT<name> (with interaction = TRUE) is how that change varies with temperature. These are the names brms estimates and that build_hazard_prior sets priors on. c<name> is a continuous dose term: with three or more stressor levels it is a per-scale slope through them, but with only two it cannot be told apart from a per-treatment shift of the amplitude loga. A main effect on its own is in fact just that shift: it is equivalent to a covariate on the amplitude, loga ~ 1 + z in build_hazard_spec's dpar_formulas. The additive dT<name> term is not: no dpar_formulas entry reproduces it, so it is the part costressor() supplies. A temperature interaction of a different shape can still be had through dpar_formulas (the multiplicative form in ‘Two kinds of temperature interaction’ below); what is unique to costressor() is this particular additive term.

Because c<name> and dT<name> are ordinary parameters, dpar_formulas in build_hazard_spec can put covariates on either, so the stressor's effect can itself vary: cDO = ~ 1 + acclim lets the oxygen sensitivity depend on acclimation (a stressor-by-covariate interaction), and the same on dT<name> lets the temperature interaction vary. These are higher-order terms, so they need a design that varies temperature, the stressor and the covariate together enough to identify them; the formula is built either way, but a thin design shows up as poor mixing rather than a clean fit.

Categorical stressor treatments

costressor() expects a stressor measured on a numeric scale, so ref, scale and direction mean something. Quantitative treatment levels belong here even though they are "treatments": dissolved oxygen dosed at 8.5, 5 and 2 mg/L is numeric, so pass the measured level as column. A genuinely unordered categorical stressor, with no scale on which a reference and a per-unit step make sense, does not. Model it through dpar_formulas in build_hazard_spec instead: a factor on the amplitude loga gives a per-treatment level shift, the same as a stressor main effect. To let the treatment effect vary with temperature, put the factor on the parameter that governs the temperature response (logb for the exponential forms, Tc for the threshold forms). That is a genuine temperature-by-treatment interaction, though a different parameterisation from the co-stressor's dT<name> term, as it scales the temperature slope rather than adding to it (see ‘Two kinds of temperature interaction’ below). A two-level treatment can instead be encoded 0/1 and passed to costressor(), which then gives the co-stressor's own main and interaction terms.

An interaction outside the temperatures of the data

The interaction is off by default because of how it behaves away from the temperatures at which individuals failed. It makes the effect of the stressor a straight line in temperature, c + dT (Ta - Tr), which is informed only over those temperatures: a few degrees, in a ramping assay. Extended below them the line reaches zero at Tr - c / dT and changes sign beyond, so a model in which the stressor is harmful where individuals failed may have it protective at cooler temperatures, such as those of a field record. Use the interaction to describe how the stressor's effect changes within the temperatures of the assay, and compare what the models with and without it imply at the temperatures a prediction is needed for (see the vignette Temperature and a co-stressor).

Two kinds of temperature interaction

The dT<name> interaction is additive on the temperature slope: it adds dT<name> * (Ta - Tr) * z to log M, so the per-degree effect shifts by a constant amount per unit of stressor. This is the standard temperature-by-stressor interaction, it works the same on every M(T) function, and it lets the slope change sign, so a stressor can in principle flatten or reverse the thermal effect. The sign of dT<name> then reads as the synergy or antagonism of temperature and the stressor (on the proportional-hazards scale): positive steepens the thermal slope, negative flattens it, and a large enough negative value reverses it (an antagonistic crossover where warming becomes protective under severe harm caused by the co-stressor). The alternative is to let the stressor rescale thermal sensitivity by a proportion, which keeps it positive: set interaction = FALSE (so the co-stressor adds only its main effect and the z_<name> column) and put that column on the sensitivity parameter through dpar_formulas instead: logb ~ 1 + z_<name> for the exponential forms (for the threshold forms a factor on Tc shifts the threshold location, a different effect). Choose the additive form for a conventional interaction and the freedom for the slope to change sign (e.g., an antagonistic crossover), the multiplicative form when the biology is a proportional change in sensitivity that should stay positive (it can attenuate the thermal slope but not reverse it).

Examples

# Dissolved oxygen held at a fixed level per trial: benign at air-saturation
# (about 8.5 mg/L), expressed per mg/L, with less oxygen meaning more stress. It
# enters through its main effect alone.
costressor("DO", column = "do", ref = 8.5, scale = 1, direction = -1)
#> $name
#> [1] "DO"
#> 
#> $column
#> [1] "do"
#> 
#> $ref
#> [1] 8.5
#> 
#> $scale
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $direction
#> [1] -1
#> 
#> $interaction
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $trajectory
#> NULL
#> 
#> $transform
#> NULL
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "rTFT_costressor"

# The same with its interaction with temperature.
costressor("DO", column = "do", ref = 8.5, scale = 1, direction = -1,
           interaction = TRUE)
#> $name
#> [1] "DO"
#> 
#> $column
#> [1] "do"
#> 
#> $ref
#> [1] 8.5
#> 
#> $scale
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $direction
#> [1] -1
#> 
#> $interaction
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $trajectory
#> NULL
#> 
#> $transform
#> NULL
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "rTFT_costressor"

# A toxicant that changes over the trial, supplied as its own trajectory.
tox_path <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = c(0, 60), conc = c(0, 4))
costressor("Tox", column = "conc", ref = 0, scale = 1, direction = 1,
           trajectory = tox_path)
#> $name
#> [1] "Tox"
#> 
#> $column
#> [1] "conc"
#> 
#> $ref
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $scale
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $direction
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $interaction
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $trajectory
#>   path_id time conc
#> 1       A    0    0
#> 2       A   60    4
#> 
#> $transform
#> NULL
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "rTFT_costressor"

# Salinity, harmful above or below an optimum: a squared standardised deviation
# makes z measure distance from the optimum (about 15 PSU, per 5 PSU) in either
# direction. With a transform supplied, `direction` no longer applies.
costressor("Sal", column = "sal", ref = 15, scale = 5, direction = 1,
           transform = function(u) u^2)
#> $name
#> [1] "Sal"
#> 
#> $column
#> [1] "sal"
#> 
#> $ref
#> [1] 15
#> 
#> $scale
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> $direction
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $interaction
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $trajectory
#> NULL
#> 
#> $transform
#> function (u) 
#> u^2
#> <environment: 0x55d01cb10f28>
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "rTFT_costressor"
